newsitem.title: INDIA: India says tax cuts can spur capital formation.
newsitem.headline: India says tax cuts can spur capital formation.

text.p: Indian Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia said on Thursday that corporate tax cuts proposed in last week's federal budget for 1997/98 (April-March) could spur increased capital formation and fuel growth.

"Revenue growth of around 16 percent can be achieved in spite of a cut in tax rates," Ahluwalia told a meeting of businessmen of the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry (Assocham) in the Indian capital.
If this is achieved, fiscal deficit would be under control, and at the same time serve as an incentive to invest, he said.
"It will support much higher rates of capital formation," Ahluwalia, the most senior civil servant in the Finance Ministry said.
India aims to cut fiscal deficit to 4.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997/98, after closing the current 1996/97 fiscal at 5.0 percent.
The budget announced by the centre-left United Front coalition government proposed to cut corporate tax to 35 percent from 40 percent in a move that surpassed industry's expectations.
Net tax revenue in 1997/98 has been projected at 1133.93 billion rupees ($31.6 billion), up 16.6 percent from an expected 972.12 billion in 1996/97.
"I think the budget as a whole is a sign of confidence," Ahluwalia said.
International investors had come to believe that there was a much deeper consensus on the economic reform programme launched in 1991, he said.
The Congress party had launched the reforms, which are being continued by the successor government after the Congress lost power in general elections last year.
"I think external circumstances are quite favourable. With a bit of luck, India's long-term growth rate environment will be seen as seven percent. That is no mean achievement," Ahluwalia said.
India expects GDP to grow by 7.0 percent or more in 1997/98, after closing 1996/97 with 6.8 percent.
